0.title: The Lord Reigns over All
0.essay:
The proudest king of the ancient world once walked on the roof of his palace and said to himself, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built?” Within the hour he was driven out to eat grass like an ox. When his reason returned, Nebuchadnezzar had learned the lesson this study is about: God “does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand” (Daniel 4:35).

Who is in charge?

Every life rests on an answer to that question, spoken or not. Some say chance, some say fate, some say the strongest, some say me. Scripture says, “Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases” (Psalm 115:3). Nothing lies outside his rule: not the stars, not the nations, not the smallest sparrow, not the worst evil, not the salvation of a single sinner.

A doctrine for the anxious

The sovereignty of God is sometimes treated as a puzzle for theologians, or a weapon for arguments. In the Bible it is neither. It is a pillow for the anxious, a spur to the timid and a reason for worship. David, hunted and betrayed, prayed, “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15). That is what this doctrine is for: to put our times, our fears and our futures into the hands of the one who holds everything.

The chapters

What It Means That God Is Sovereign; Creation and Providence — God upholding and governing all things; History, Nations and Evil; Sovereign in Salvation; Sovereignty and Human Responsibility; and Living Under a Sovereign God. It belongs alongside the studies on God’s attributes and his providence.

1.title: What It Means That God Is Sovereign
1.essay:
To say that God is sovereign is to say that he is King — not a figurehead, not a constitutional monarch, but the one who actually rules. “The LORD has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all” (Psalm 103:19).

The only Sovereign

Paul calls God “the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Timothy 6:15). His rule has three marks. It is universal: it covers all things, great and small. It is powerful: Jeremiah prayed, “Nothing is too hard for you” (Jeremiah 32:17). And it is purposeful: God is not merely reacting to events, but “declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, ‘My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose’” (Isaiah 46:10). He is the one “who works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11).

Job came to the end of his long suffering with this confession: “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be thwarted” (Job 42:2). He still had no explanation for his pain. What he had was God himself, and that was enough.

What sovereignty is not

It is not fate. Fate is blind and impersonal; God is a Father who knows, loves and plans. The Stoic shrugs at what must be; the Christian trusts the one who rules.

It is not tyranny. God’s power is never separated from his goodness, wisdom and justice. He never does anything that is not right. His sovereignty is good news precisely because he is good.

And it is not mere permission. Scripture does speak of God allowing things he does not approve, but it never pictures him as a spectator, hoping things turn out well. Even what he permits, he permits on purpose, and he weaves it into his plan.

What he commands and what he decrees

Theologians distinguish two senses in which Scripture speaks of God’s will. His will of command is what he tells us to do: love him, keep his law, believe the gospel. This can be disobeyed, and often is. His will of decree is what he has purposed to happen, and it cannot fail. The two never contradict each other in God, though we cannot always see how they fit. Moses drew the line for us: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deuteronomy 29:29). We are not called to read the secret plan, but to obey the revealed word.

The king on the roof

Nebuchadnezzar had to learn this the hard way. When he was restored, he did not resent God’s rule; he praised it. Sovereignty humbles the proud and lifts up the humble, and the humbled king found it the best news he had ever heard.

A business owner who has built something from nothing can easily think like the king on the roof. This doctrine does not shame his hard work; it puts it in its place. Every gift, every opportunity and every breath came from God, and so does every success. The fitting response is not pride, but thanks.

For reflection

When you think of God’s sovereignty, do you feel comfort, fear or resistance? Why? How is God’s rule different from fate? What part of your life do you most need to put into his hands today?

2.title: Creation and Providence
2.essay:
God did not make the world and then step back to watch it run. Every moment, he holds it in being and steers it to its end. Christians have a word for this ongoing care: providence.

Holding all things

Providence has two sides. The first is preservation. The Son “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3); “he is before all things, and in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). The universe does not continue by its own momentum. If God ceased to will it, it would cease to be.

The second is government: God directs all things toward his purposes. Jesus put it in the tenderest terms: “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows” (Matthew 10:29–31). If God governs the fall of a cheap bird, he governs your life.

Nothing is chance

Even what looks most random is in his hand: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). Our lifespans are known to him — “in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them” (Psalm 139:16). So are our places in history; God has determined “allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place” for the nations (Acts 17:26).

Usually God works through ordinary means: weather, doctors, governments, friends and the natural order he made. Medicine is not opposed to providence; it is one of its instruments. Sometimes he works without means, or against them, and we call that a miracle. But providence is no less God’s work for being quiet.

Providence in Scripture’s stories

The book of Ruth never mentions a miracle. A widow from Moab simply goes to glean, and “she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz” (Ruth 2:3). The word “happened” is almost a wink to the reader: nothing just happened. From that chance meeting came David, and from David came Christ.

The book of Jonah piles up the word “appointed”. “The LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah” (Jonah 1:17); “the LORD God appointed a plant” to shade him (Jonah 4:6); and “God appointed a worm” to destroy it (Jonah 4:7). Fish, plant and worm were all servants of the same patient purpose: to teach a prophet mercy.

When Job lost his children and his wealth, he said, “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). He did not say “luck took away”, or “Satan took away”, though Satan was involved. He traced everything to the God he trusted, and he worshipped.

The missed train and the operating table

A man misses his train and fumes on the platform. Weeks later, he finds that the conversation he had while waiting led someone to Christ. Most of the time we never find out what a delay was for. Providence does not promise that we will understand, only that nothing is wasted.

A woman facing surgery prays, trusts her surgeon and follows his advice. She does not think that using medicine shows a lack of faith, or that trusting God means ignoring the doctor. She rests in the God who works through hospitals as truly as through miracles, and she leaves the outcome in his hands.

For reflection

Where have you seen God’s quiet providence in your own story? How does Jesus’ word about sparrows speak to your fears? Why is using ordinary means, like medicine, not a lack of faith?

3.title: History, Nations and Evil
3.essay:
It is one thing to believe God rules the sparrows. It is harder to believe he rules empires, elections and wars — and hardest of all to believe he rules even over evil, without being stained by it. Scripture asks us to believe all three.

The Lord of the nations

Daniel praised the God who “changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings” (Daniel 2:21). Rulers think they are in charge, but “the king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will” (Proverbs 21:1). Human plans rise and fall, while “the counsel of the LORD stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations” (Psalm 33:11).

The Bible gives startling examples. Isaiah named a Persian king a century and a half before his time: “Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus” (Isaiah 45:1). Cyrus never knew the Lord, yet he sent the exiles home. Earlier, God called Assyria “the rod of my anger” (Isaiah 10:5) to discipline his people. But Assyria had its own plans: “he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think” (Isaiah 10:7). It meant only conquest, and when God had finished using it, he punished it for its arrogance (Isaiah 10:12).

Evil in the hand of God

This is the hardest part. If God rules all things, does he rule evil too? Scripture says yes — and insists, just as firmly, that God is never the author of sin. “God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one” (James 1:13). Evil is always the act of creatures, and they are always guilty of it. Yet God is never defeated by it; he takes the worst that is done and bends it to his good purposes.

Joseph’s brothers sold him into slavery. Years later he said to them, “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today” (Genesis 50:20). The same event had two authors with opposite intentions. The brothers were wicked; God was good. Both meant it.

The cross

The clearest case of all is the death of Jesus. Peter told the crowd in Jerusalem that Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God,” and in the same breath, “you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). The early church prayed that Herod, Pilate and the rulers had gathered “to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28). The greatest crime in history was also the greatest act of love. If God could rule that day, he can rule any day.

Jesus himself told Pilate, “You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). And Psalm 2 shows the nations raging against God and his anointed, while “he who sits in the heavens laughs” (Psalm 2:4). Their rebellion cannot overturn his plan.

Where our understanding stops

We cannot fully explain how God rules evil without doing evil. Paul did not try either. After three chapters on God’s purposes he broke into praise: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33). Humility is the right response, not a cleverer theory.

For the wounded and the worried

This truth must be handled with great care. A survivor of abuse should never be told that what was done to her was good. It was evil, and the one who did it is guilty before God. What she can be told, gently and in time, is that God has not lost control, that he will judge what was done, and that he is able to bring good even out of this, as he did for Joseph. That is not a quick fix. It is a firm floor.

Believers living under a hostile government can take heart too. No regime is outside God’s reach. The rulers of Psalm 2 rage, but the Lord reigns; and the gospel has outlasted every empire that tried to crush it.

For reflection

How does God’s rule over the nations change how you watch the news? How can God rule evil without being its author? Where have you seen God bring good out of something that was meant for harm?

4.title: Sovereign in Salvation
4.essay:
If God rules sparrows and kings, does he also rule the turning of a human heart to himself? Scripture answers with a word many find difficult and many more have found precious: election.

Chosen before the world began

Paul begins Ephesians with a burst of praise for the God who “chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will” (Ephesians 1:4–5). In Romans he traces an unbreakable chain: “those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:30). No one drops out between the links.

God said to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion,” and Paul concludes: “So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy” (Romans 9:15–16). Jesus himself thanked his Father that he had hidden these things “from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will” (Matthew 11:25–26).

Two ways of reading it

Christians who love the Bible have read these texts differently. The Arminian view holds that God elects those he foresees will believe. Election is real, but it rests on God’s foreknowledge of a free human choice, and grace can be resisted to the end. This view wants to protect human responsibility and God’s love for all.

The Reformed view holds that God chose his people freely, not because of anything he saw in them, and that his grace effectively brings them to faith. Faith is the fruit of election, not its cause.

This study comes down on the Reformed side, because that is where the texts most naturally lead. God saved us “not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began” (2 Timothy 1:9). Salvation “depends not on human will or exertion” (Romans 9:16). And when Paul preached in Pisidian Antioch, “as many as were appointed to eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48) — the appointing came first. Still, the debate is among brothers and sisters, and both sides confess that salvation is by grace alone.

What election is for

Election is always in Christ. God does not choose people apart from his Son, but to be united to him. It is never a reason for pride, since it rests on nothing in us. It is never a reason for laziness either: God chose us “that we should be holy” (Ephesians 1:4). And it is never a reason to stop evangelising. Paul said, “I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory” (2 Timothy 2:10). In Corinth, when he was discouraged, the Lord told him, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you … for I have many in this city who are my people” (Acts 18:9–10). Election made Paul bolder, not quieter.

“What if I am not chosen?”

Some people lie awake over this question. The answer is not to peer into God’s secret decree, but to look at Christ’s open invitation: “All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). The first half of that verse is election; the second half is a promise to you. If you come to Christ, you will not be turned away — and your coming is the evidence that the Father gave you to him.

A missionary’s confidence

A missionary has laboured for years among a people with almost no converts. What keeps her going is not her own skill but God’s promise: “so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty” (Isaiah 55:11). God has his people among every tribe and tongue, and he will call them. Her task is to keep speaking.

For reflection

How does election in Christ humble you? Why should it make you bolder in evangelism, not less? If you have ever worried that you are not chosen, how does John 6:37 answer you?

5.title: Sovereignty and Human Responsibility
5.essay:
If God has planned everything, do our choices matter? Scripture never lets us drop either truth. God is completely sovereign, and we are completely responsible. The Bible teaches both, often in the same breath, and expects us to live by both.

The shipwreck

On Paul’s voyage to Rome, an angel promised him that no one would die: “there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship” (Acts 27:22). God had decided. Yet a few hours later, when the sailors tried to escape in the lifeboat, Paul said, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved” (Acts 27:31). God’s promise did not make the sailors’ actions pointless; it worked through them. Paul saw no contradiction, and neither should we.

Both at once

Proverbs puts it simply: “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). We plan; God directs. Paul tells the Philippians to “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). Notice the word “for”. God’s work in us is not a reason to stop working; it is the reason we can work at all.

James warns against planning as if we were in control. Instead we should say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:15). That is not a refusal to plan; it is planning with open hands.

How can both be true?

Theologians call this view compatibilism: God’s sovereignty and real human choice are compatible. God does not force people against their wills like puppets. He works in and through their desires, so that they freely do what he has purposed. How he does this is beyond us, but that he does it is the plain teaching of Scripture.

When someone objects, as Paul’s readers did, “Why does he still find fault?”, Paul does not offer a philosophical system. He answers, “But who are you, O man, to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20). That is not an evasion. It is a reminder that creatures cannot stand over their Creator and demand that he explain himself.

Prayer and evangelism matter

Some think sovereignty makes prayer pointless. The opposite is true. God has ordained not only ends but means, and prayer is one of his chosen means. We pray because he rules; if he did not, there would be no one to pray to. The same goes for evangelism. God has his people, and he calls them through the preaching of the gospel. Our witness is not wasted effort; it is the very way he brings them home.

Mordecai urged Esther to go to the king: “And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14). He was sure deliverance would come; he still called her to act. God’s plan does not make our obedience optional. It gives it meaning.

In ordinary life

Students are not excused from revising because God knows their results. They study hard and trust God with the outcome, and they are free from the crushing idea that everything depends on them.

A church planning outreach prays as though everything depends on God and works as though everything depends on them — which, in different ways, is true. A father weighing a move for his family seeks advice, counts the cost, prays and decides. He then goes forward in peace, knowing that his steps are established by the Lord even when his plans change.

For reflection

Where do you tend to lean too far — passivity (“God will do it”) or anxiety (“it all depends on me”)? How does God’s sovereignty make prayer more meaningful, not less? What decision are you facing where you need to plan with open hands?

6.title: Living Under a Sovereign God
6.essay:
The sovereignty of God is not only something to believe; it is somewhere to live. It changes how we face suffering, how we handle success, how we pray and how we look at the future.

Comfort in suffering

“And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). Paul does not say all things are good; many are not. He says that God works them together for good. And the next verse tells us what that good is: to be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). God’s goal is not our comfort but our Christlikeness, and nothing we suffer is outside that purpose.

Paul could even call his sufferings “this light momentary affliction” which is “preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 4:17). He was not making light of pain; he was weighing it against glory.

Freedom from anxiety

Jesus told his disciples not to worry about what they would eat or wear, because “your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32). Anxiety often comes from believing that we must hold everything together. The sovereign God invites us to put that weight down: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10).

When God’s ways make no sense to us, we remember that “as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts” (Isaiah 55:9). Trust does not need to understand everything. It needs to know who is in charge.

Boldness in witness

When the apostles were threatened by the authorities, the church prayed, “Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them” (Acts 4:24). They reminded themselves that even their persecutors could only do what God’s plan allowed (Acts 4:28). Then they asked not for safety but for courage: “grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness” (Acts 4:29). The place shook, and they went out and spoke.

Humility in success

David, at the height of his reign, prayed, “Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all. In your hand are power and might” (1 Chronicles 29:12). A businesswoman whose company is thriving can pray the same. Sovereignty guards success from pride, just as it guards suffering from despair.

Worship

Above all, the sovereignty of God leads to worship. Paul ends his long discussion of God’s purposes with a doxology: “For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen” (Romans 11:36). In Revelation 4 John sees the throne of heaven with every creature bowing before it. And at the end of history a great multitude cries, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns” (Revelation 19:6).

Reading the end of the book

A man receives a hard diagnosis. He grieves, and he is afraid. But he prays Psalm 31 — “My times are in your hand” — and he finds that he can sleep. His illness is real, but it is not in charge.

An old preacher was asked whether he was worried about the state of the world. He replied, “No. I have read the end of the book.” That is what the sovereignty of God gives us: not every answer, but the last chapter. The Lord reigns, and he will make all things new.

For reflection

Which area of your life most needs the comfort of God’s sovereignty right now? How does it guard you against both pride and despair? Read Revelation 4 and 19 aloud, and turn what you read into praise.
